en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on Garlic 1.
The Training Rule on Garlic:
Now, venerable ladies, these one hundred and sixty-six rules of expiation come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain lay follower had invited the community of bhikkhunīs to garlic, saying:
“Venerable ladies, for whichever of you there is need of garlic, I have garlic.”
And the field-guard was instructed:
"If bhikkhunīs come, give two or three bundles to each bhikkhunī.
Now at that time, there was a festival in Sāvatthī.
The garlic that had been brought there came to an end.
The bhikkhunīs approached that lay follower and said to him,
"Friend, we have need of garlic."
“There is none, Venerable Lady.
The garlic we were supplied has been completely used up.
Please go to the field.”
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā went to a field and, not knowing moderation, had a great quantity of garlic carried away.
The field-guardian complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can these bhikkhunīs, not knowing moderation, have such a great quantity of garlic carried away?"
The bhikkhunīs heard that field-guard complaining, grumbling, and resenting [the matter].
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and resented, saying:
"How can the noble lady Thullanandā, failing to know moderation, have so much garlic carried away?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā, not knowing moderation, had much garlic carried away?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her … [as before] …
"How indeed, monks, could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, without knowing moderation, have garlic carried away in such great quantities?
This, monks, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus."
“Once upon a time, monks, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was the wife of a certain brahmin.
They had three daughters:
Nandā, Nandavatī, and Sundarīnandā.”
Then, monks, after that brahmin had passed away, he was reborn in a certain swan-womb.
All his feathers were made of pure gold.
He would give one feather from each of them.
Then, monks, the nun Thullanandā, thinking, “This swan gives us each a feather,” seized that king of swans and plucked him until he was featherless.
As his feathers grew back again, they turned out to be white.
Even then, monks, through excessive greed, the nun Thullanandā was deprived of her golden complexion.
"Now the garlic will run out.
One should be content with what has been obtained,
for excessive greed is evil.
“Having taken the king of swans, you have fallen away from your golden [beauty].
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the bhikkhunī Thullanandā in many ways for her greediness... [and so forth].
And thus, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:
“Whichever bhikkhunī should eat garlic, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Whichever, moreover, means:
Whichever [nun] of whatever kind... [pe] ...a bhikkhunī...
[pe] ...this is the bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Garlic" refers to that which is called Māgadhaka.
"If one receives it with the intention, 'I will eat it,'" there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every swallow, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats garlic while perceiving it as garlic, there is an offense of expiation.
If one eats garlic while being uncertain about it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one eats garlic while perceiving it as garlic, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one eats garlic that is not garlic while perceiving it as garlic, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one eats garlic that is not garlic while being doubtful about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is garlic, and she perceives it as garlic, and she eats it, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of onions.
Bhañjanaka,
harītaka,
and cāpala-garlic.
In the cooking of broth,
the cooking of meat,
and the cooking of oil.
In the case of Sāḷavā,
in the case of Uttaribhaṅgā,
and in the case of one who is insane.
"By the first offender":
thus the training rule on garlic is concluded for the first time.
